title: Reading a Science Article II: Correlation vs. Causation & Data in Text
goal: Tell the difference between "two things happen together" and "one causes the other"; read a percentage, a described graph, or a statistic used inside an argument and judge whether it actually supports the claim built on top of it.

prompts: From memory: what three questions does a scientific reader ask of a study (Session 4)?
What went wrong with the GlowGuard press release specifically?

vocab.def: when two things tend to change together (as one goes up, the other tends to go up or down too)
when one thing actually makes the other happen. Establishing causation usually needs a controlled experiment, not just an observed pattern

facts: almost any two things that both rise and fall with the seasons, the economy, or a population's growth will show some correlation, whether or not either one causes the other.
journalists and advertisers both have an incentive to state a correlation as if it were a proven cause, because "X causes Y" is a much more compelling sentence than "X and Y happen to move together."
prime.question: recall a headline you've seen that claimed one thing "causes" another — would "is linked to" have been the more honest word?
prime.intro: Two facts before you read: (1) almost any two things that both rise and fall with the seasons, the economy, or a population's growth will show some correlation, whether or not either one causes the other. (2) journalists and advertisers both have an incentive to state a correlation as if it were a proven cause, because "X causes Y" is a much more compelling sentence than "X and Y happen to move together." Orienting question: recall a headline you've seen that claimed one thing "causes" another — would "is linked to" have been the more honest word?

write.task: Write a paragraph (5–7 sentences): pick either the ice-cream/drowning or speed-camera example and explain what would need to be true for the causal claim to actually be well-supported (e.g., a controlled trial: cameras installed on some streets and not others, similar in every other way, compared over the same period). Use correlation, causation, and confounding variable correctly at least once each.

items.q: Compare your answers with the model answer.
items.a: since city-wide accidents fell ~25% with no cameras anywhere, at most roughly 15 percentage points of Elm Street's 40% drop (40 − 25) can plausibly be attributed to the cameras specifically — and even that residual could still be explained by the stop sign or the school closure, so the honest answer is "the cameras may have helped some, but this data cannot show how much, or whether they helped at all."

items.q: Can you correctly identify the confounding variable in both examples without rereading, and explain in one sentence why "correlation" alone never proves "causation"?

passages.title: A real, classic example
paragraphs: Every summer, two numbers rise together in most countries with cold winters: ice cream sales and the number of people who drown. Track this across any year and the two lines climb and fall in almost the same shape, month by month. If you only looked at the correlation, you could write a headline: "Ice Cream Sales Linked to Drowning Deaths" — and it would be, strictly, true: the two numbers do correlate.

Nobody seriously believes ice cream causes drowning, or that drowning makes people crave ice cream. The real explanation is a confounding variable: hot weather. Hot weather makes people buy more ice cream, and hot weather also makes far more people go swimming — which is when almost all drownings happen. Ice cream and drowning are correlated only because they share a common cause; neither one causes the other at all.

This example is famous precisely because it's obvious once explained — which is exactly why it's useful. The same structure hides inside far less obvious, far more consequential claims: a study might find that people who take a particular vitamin have fewer heart attacks, and a headline might imply the vitamin protects the heart — when the real explanation could be that people who already exercise, don't smoke, and see a doctor regularly are more likely to take vitamins in the first place, and it's the exercise and non-smoking doing the protective work, not the pill.

questions.q: Think question: the passage says this "hides inside far less obvious... claims." Why is an obvious example like ice cream/drowning actually more useful for learning the pattern than a realistic-but-murky one would be on its own?

passages.title: Data in text
paragraphs: A local news segment reports: "Since the new speed cameras went up on Elm Street last year, accidents are down 40%! Clearly the cameras are working." What the segment does not mention: Elm Street also had a new stop sign installed the same month, a nearby school closed (cutting morning traffic by roughly a third), and the city-wide accident rate — across streets with no cameras at all — also fell about 25% that year, likely due to a mild winter with less ice.

questions.q: What is the segment's causal claim, and what's the correlation it's actually built on?

Given the city-wide 25% drop with no cameras anywhere, roughly how much of Elm Street's 40% drop might the cameras actually explain — all of it, none of it, or something in between? Defend your estimate using the numbers given.

moves.title: the correlation/causation check
paragraphs: Whenever a text claims "A causes B," ask three questions: (1) Is this actually a controlled experiment (one thing was deliberately changed, everything else held constant), or just two numbers that happened to move together over time? (2) Could B actually cause A instead (the arrow reversed)? (3) Is there a confounding variable driving both A and B independently?
